Warfarin is an anticoagulant medicine that stops blood clotting.
Warfarin is only available with a prescription.
What is warfarin used for?
Warfarin is often prescribed for people who have had a condition caused by a
blood clot
. This includes:
a
stroke
a
heart attack
deep vein thrombosis
– a blood clot within a deep vein in the body
a pulmonary embolism – a blood clot in the lungs
Warfarin may also be prescribed for people at an increased risk of developing harmful blood clots. For example, people with a blood clotting disorder like thrombophilia.
How to take warfarin
Warfarin helps to decrease the blood’s tendency to clot, without stopping it completely. This means your warfarin dose must be carefully monitored. If necessary, it’ll be adjusted.
You’ll have regular
blood tests
to make sure that your dose is correct.
It’s very important that you take warfarin exactly as directed. Don’t increase your prescribed dose unless the doctor in charge of your care advises you to.
Warfarin should be taken once a day, usually in the evening. Take your dose at the same time each day before, during or after a meal.
How long you’ll need to take warfarin will depend on what it’s been prescribed for. Ask the healthcare professional responsible for your care if you’re not sure.
Do
take extra care to avoid cutting yourself
take care when shaving
brush your teeth carefully
wear protective clothing when gardening, sewing or playing contact sports
use insect repellent to avoid insect bites or stings
Missed or extra doses
If you usually take warfarin in the morning and forget to take it at your normal time, take it as soon as you remember. You should then continue taking it as normal.
If it’s time to take your next dose, don’t take a double dose to catch up unless your GP advises you to.
If you forget to take your dose of warfarin in the evening but remember before midnight on the same day, take the missed dose.
If midnight has passed, leave that dose and take your normal dose the next day at the usual time.
Ask your GP practice or local anticoagulant clinic if you’re not sure what to do about a missed dose of warfarin. You can also phone
111
for advice.
Possible side effects
Bleeding is the main side effect associated with warfarin. This is because the medicine slows down the blood’s normal clotting ability.
You’re more at risk of bleeding in the first few weeks of starting treatment with warfarin. You’re also at risk when you’re unwell.
Skin rashes and hair loss are also common side effects of warfarin.
You should speak to your GP practice or healthcare professional if you experience side effects when taking warfarin.
Phone 999 or go to A&E if:
You’re taking warfarin and you:
have a
fall
or accident
experience a significant blow to your head
are unable to stop any bleeding
Phone 111 if:
You’re taking warfarin and you have:
blood in your pee or poo
poo that’s black
severe bruising
nosebleeds
lasting more than 10 minutes
bleeding gums
been coughing up blood or have blood in your vomit
unusual
headaches
changes to your menstrual cycle, if you have one, such as heavy or increased bleeding during your period, or any other bleeding from your vagina
Warnings and precautions
Some people will be advised not to take warfarin. This includes:
pregnant women – it can affect the development of the baby
people with uncontrolled
high blood pressure
people with a high risk of internal bleeding – for example, those with a
stomach ulcer
people with a bleeding disorder like haemophilia
Other medicines and warfarin
Warfarin can interact with many other medicines. The patient information leaflet should tell you if a medication is safe to take with warfarin. You should ask your pharmacist or GP practice if you’re unsure.
When taking warfarin:
don’t take
aspirin
, or treatments containing aspirin, unless it’s prescribed by a healthcare professional as it could cause bleeding
don’t take
ibuprofen
unless it’s prescribed by a healthcare professional
You can take
paracetamol
, but don’t take more than the recommended dose.
Herbal medicines and supplements can also interact with warfarin. You should avoid taking them without first checking with a healthcare professional.
Food and drink
Vitamin K
Some food and drink can interfere with the effect of warfarin if consumed in large amounts, including foods that are rich in vitamin K.
Foods containing large amounts of vitamin K include:
green leafy vegetables, including broccoli, spinach and lettuce
chickpeas
liver
egg yolks
mature cheese and blue cheese
avocado
olive oil
Small amounts of vitamin K can also be found in meat and dairy foods.
When your first dose of warfarin is prescribed, it doesn’t matter how much vitamin K you’re eating because the dosage will be based on your current blood clotting levels.
However, if you make significant changes to your diet, such as increasing your vitamin K intake or cutting out foods that contain vitamin K, it could interfere with how warfarin works.
You should speak to your healthcare professional before making changes to your diet while taking warfarin. They’ll also be able to give you more information about foods to avoid or limit.
Cranberry and grapefruit juice
Do not drink cranberry or grapefruit juice while you’re taking warfarin. It can increase the effect of your medicine and put you at higher risk of bleeding.
Alcohol
Getting drunk or binge drinking is dangerous while taking warfarin. It may increase the effect of the medicine and the risk of bleeding.
Read low-risk drinking guidelines
Heavy drinkers or people with liver disease who are taking warfarin shouldn’t drink alcohol.
Surgery and dental work
Your dose of warfarin may need to be lowered or stopped a few days before having an operation or dental work. This is due to the risk of bleeding.
Tell the surgeon or dentist that you’re taking warfarin. You should also tell anyone else involved with your care, like an anticoagulant nurse, if you need an operation.
Vaccinations
You can have vaccinations while taking warfarin, but all injections must:
be given under the skin
not be given into the muscle as it may cause bruising
have firm pressure applied to the site for 10 minutes afterwards
Playing sports
You can play some sports while taking warfarin. Due to the risk of bleeding, you should avoid some sports while taking warfarin. This includes:
contact sports that could lead to a head injury, like football, rugby, cricket and hockey
martial arts
kickboxing
You can continue to take part in non-contact sports, like:
running
athletics
cycling
racquet sports
Make sure you wear protective clothing like a cycle helmet.
Holidays
Tell your GP or anticoagulant nurse if you’re going on holiday in this country or abroad. You should arrange to have your blood checked before you go.
If you’re going to be away longer than a month, you may need to arrange to have your blood checked while you’re away.
Make sure you have enough warfarin tablets to last for the duration of your trip.
Body piercings
Body piercings aren’t recommended while taking warfarin. There’s an increased risk of bleeding and infection.
